    Creating selectors¶

    This notebook explains the selector contract in full detail and shows how to implement, validate and consume a custom selector.

    Selectors are the objects that decide which rows of the data receive a deficit (outlier / missing value / noise / drift / drop). A generator that accepts a selector delegates the who to the selector and keeps the what to itself.

    Goal¶

    Write a custom selector: the score contract (which rows a deficit is affected by), the preset implementations, and how generators turn the scores into deficits.

    The contract¶

    A selector is any callable with the signature:

    selector(X, y) -> dict[str, array]

    with, per variable (usually a column of X, resolved via column_mapping):

    • a boolean mask (True = deficit applied to that row), or
    • a float score in [0, 1] — the probability that the deficit is applied (1.0 = definitely, 0.0 = never). Boolean masks are simply the degenerate deterministic case of that contract.

    How generators turn scores into deficits¶

    A score only says how likely each row is to be affected — it does not apply anything. Turning it into an actual deficit is the consuming generator's job, and the mechanism depends on the deficit type:

    • shape-preserving generators (noise, drift, missingness) keep every row and decide per row whether the deficit is applied: a row with score 0.3 is affected in 30% of the draws (Bernoulli firing);
    • row-removing generators (imbalance) remove rows: a row's score becomes its weight in the resampling — 1 - score is the probability that the row is kept, so high-score rows disappear more often.
    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from numpy.random import default_rng

from badgers.core.selectors import AlwaysSelector, BernoulliSelector, ProportionalSelector

rng = default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(100, 2))
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np from numpy.random import default_rng from badgers.core.selectors import AlwaysSelector, BernoulliSelector, ProportionalSelector rng = default_rng(0) X = rng.normal(size=(100, 2))

    Comparing the bundled selectors¶

    All three bundled selectors below act on the same single column, f0 (column 0 of X). The helper _plot_selector_scores draws one panel per selector so they can be compared side by side on the same rows: the first axis shows the f0 column (sorted) as a reference for the row order, the next three are the selectors applied to those rows.

    Selector Score type What the panel shows
    AlwaysSelector boolean mask every row affected
    BernoulliSelector(rate=0.3) boolean mask a random ~30% of rows
    ProportionalSelector float score deficit probability rising with f0

    Boolean masks draw red for affected rows, green for untouched ones; float scores use a red-to-green colormap (red = high deficit probability).

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    def _plot_selector_scores(selectors, X, title):
    """One panel per selector over X; bool masks drawn red/green,
    float scores with a red-to-green colormap. The first axis shows
    the f0 reference column."""
    n_sel = len(selectors)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n_sel + 1, figsize=(3.2 * (n_sel + 1), 3.2), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    f0 = X[:, 0]
    order = np.argsort(f0)
    axes[0].scatter(f0[order], np.arange(len(order)), c=f0[order], cmap='viridis', s=15)
    axes[0].set_title('f0 (sorted)')
    axes[0].set_xlabel('f0 value')
    axes[0].set_ylabel('row index')
    for ax, (name, sel) in zip(axes[1:], selectors):
        out = sel(X, None)
        scores = np.asarray(list(out.values()), dtype=float).T if isinstance(out, dict) else out
        if scores.ndim == 2:
            scores = scores[:, 0]
        if scores.dtype == bool:
            colors = np.where(scores, 'C3', 'C2')
            ax.scatter(f0, np.arange(len(f0)), c=colors, s=15)
        else:
            # probability-valued scores (sum to 1) collapse to ~0 on a
            # 0..1 scale — scale per selector so the gradient is visible
            hi = scores.max()
            sc = ax.scatter(f0, np.arange(len(f0)), c=scores, cmap='RdYlGn_r', vmin=0, vmax=hi, s=15)
            fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label=f'score (max {hi:.3f})')
        ax.set_title(name)
        ax.set_xlabel('f0 value')
    fig.suptitle(title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    return fig


_ = _plot_selector_scores(
    [('AlwaysSelector', AlwaysSelector(['f0'])),
     ('BernoulliSelector(rate=0.3)', BernoulliSelector(['f0'], rate=0.3, rng=default_rng(1))),
     ('ProportionalSelector', ProportionalSelector(['f0'], column_mapping={'f0': 0}))],
    X,
    'Bundled selectors over the same rows')

    Building a custom selector¶

    The minimal recipe — a class with __call__(self, X, y, **kw) returning a {variable: values} dict. We build a threshold selector: select rows whose reference column exceeds a constructor-time threshold.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    class ThresholdSelector:
    """Select rows whose reference column exceeds a fixed threshold.

    Returns a BOOLEAN mask (deterministic case of the contract).
    """

    def __init__(self, variables, column_mapping, threshold=0.0):
        self.variables = list(variables)
        self.column_mapping = column_mapping
        self.threshold = threshold
        unknown = [v for v in self.variables if v not in column_mapping]
        if unknown:
            raise ValueError(f"variables not in column_mapping: {unknown}")

    def __call__(self, X, y=None):
        out = {}
        for v in self.variables:
            col = X[:, self.column_mapping[v]]
            out[v] = col > self.threshold
        return out

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"ThresholdSelector({self.variables!r}, threshold={self.threshold})"


sel = ThresholdSelector(['f0'], column_mapping={'f0': 0}, threshold=1.0)
X = default_rng(0).normal(size=(100, 2))
values = sel(X, None)
print(sel)
print('dtype:', values['f0'].dtype, '| affected:', int(values['f0'].sum()))
    class ThresholdSelector: """Select rows whose reference column exceeds a fixed threshold. Returns a BOOLEAN mask (deterministic case of the contract).     ThresholdSelector(['f0'], threshold=1.0)
dtype: bool | affected: 14

    A score-returning variant¶

    Now the probabilistic flavor: instead of a mask we return the probability that each row is affected. We make it a smooth function of the reference column — the further above the threshold, the closer to 1.0. Notice the selector draws no randomness.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    def sigmoid(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))


class SmoothThresholdSelector:
    """Scores: P(deficit) = sigmoid((col - threshold) / slope)."""

    def __init__(self, variables, column_mapping, threshold=0.0, slope=1.0):
        self.variables = list(variables)
        self.column_mapping = column_mapping
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.slope = slope

    def __call__(self, X, y=None):
        out = {}
        for v in self.variables:
            col = X[:, self.column_mapping[v]]
            scores = sigmoid((col - self.threshold) / self.slope)
            assert np.all((scores >= 0) & (scores <= 1))
            out[v] = scores
        return out


sel = SmoothThresholdSelector(['f0'], column_mapping={'f0': 0}, threshold=0.0, slope=0.5)
values = sel(X, None)['f0']
print('range:', values.min(), '...', values.max())
print('monotone in reference column:', np.all(np.diff(values[np.argsort(X[:, 0])]) >= 0))
    def sigmoid(z): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z)) class SmoothThresholdSelector: """Scores: P(deficit) = sigmoid((col - threshold) / slope).""" def __init__(self, variables, column_mapping, threshold=0.0, slope=1.0): self.variables = list(variables) self.column_mapping = column_mapping self.threshold = threshold self.slope = slope def __call__(self, X, y=None): out = {} for v in self.variables: col = X[:, self.column_mapping[v]] scores = sigmoid((col - self.threshold) / self.slope) assert np.all((scores >= 0) & (scores <= 1)) out[v] = scores return out sel = SmoothThresholdSelector(['f0'], column_mapping={'f0': 0}, threshold=0.0, slope=0.5) values = sel(X, None)['f0'] print('range:', values.min(), '...', values.max()) print('monotone in reference column:', np.all(np.diff(values[np.argsort(X[:, 0])]) >= 0)) 
    range: 0.008743976272339568 ... 0.9745192926928778
monotone in reference column: True

_ = _plot_selector_scores(

    Consuming the selector with a real generator¶

    Selectors are only useful through generators.

    Below we use our SmoothThresholdSelector (scores) with the RandomSamplingTargetsGenerator and verify that the resampled rows skew toward low-score rows.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    from badgers.generators.tabular_data.imbalance import RandomSamplingTargetsGenerator

# A ROW-REMOVING generator: turns fractional scores into keep-weights.
# It resamples `size` rows with replacement, weighted by (1 - score):
# rows with a LOW deficit probability (score ~ 0) are likely kept/replicated,
# rows with a HIGH score (deficit) are under-sampled.
rng = default_rng(0)
sel = SmoothThresholdSelector(['f0'], column_mapping={'f0': 0}, threshold=0.0, slope=0.5)
Xw = default_rng(1).normal(size=(200, 2))
gen = RandomSamplingTargetsGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt, _ = gen.generate(Xw, y=None, selector=sel, size=100)

scores = sel(Xw, None)['f0']
print('input rows:', len(Xw), '-> resampled rows:', len(Xt))
print('population mean f0:', Xw[:, 0].mean().round(3))
print('resampled mean f0: ', Xt[:, 0].mean().round(3), '(skewed toward low-score rows)')
assert Xt[:, 0].mean() < Xw[:, 0].mean()

population mean f0: -0.137
resampled mean f0:  -0.696 (skewed toward low-score rows)

    Conformance checklist¶

    Before contributing a selector, check:

    • constructor validates variables/column_mapping and raises clearly;
    • __call__ accepts (X, y);
    • returned dict covers exactly the declared variables;
    • boolean outputs are np.bool_ arrays; score outputs stay in [0, 1] (assert internally);

    Takeaways¶

    • A selector returns per-row scores: boolean masks (deterministic) or floats in [0, 1] (deficit probabilities).
    • Selectors never draw randomness for their rates; the consuming generator realizes them.
    • Presets (AlwaysSelector, BernoulliSelector, TopQuantileSelector, ...) cover the common cases.
